title: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
hookLine: no pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour creation began; only the Creator knows (Japji 21)

cards: A kid at the dinner table asks: when did the world start? What day? What time?
The adults look at each other. Someone mentions the Big Bang. Someone else says it depends who you ask.
Everybody's guessing. Pauri 21 asks that exact question, very precisely, and then gives an answer that's both humble and bold.

teach.h: WHAT HOUR, WHAT DAY, WHAT MONTH?
teach.b: Here's how the question is asked, in paraphrase. What was that moment, what was the hour? What lunar day, what day of the week?
What season, what month, when the form of the world came to be? A birth certificate for the universe. Then Guru Nanak goes around the room of his day.
The pandits, the Hindu scholars, didn't find the time; if they had, it would be written in the Puranas.
The qazis, the Muslim judges and scholars, didn't find the moment; if they had, they would have written it in the Qur'an.

teach.h: NO PANDIT, QAZI OR YOGI KNOWS.
teach.b: The yogi doesn't know the day or the weekday. No one knows the season or the month. Then the answer, in the original: jaa kartaa sirathee kau saaje aape jaanai soee.
The Maker who shaped creation, He alone knows. Notice how even-handed it is: pandits, qazis, yogis, the learned of the communities around Guru Nanak. It mocks none of them.
It simply says: this is beyond all of us.

teach.h: THE HONESTY TO SAY I DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: how can I speak of it, how praise it, how describe it, how know it? Everyone speaks, each trying to be wiser than the next. Great is the Master, great is His Name.
And whoever thinks they're something on their own won't be honored in the end. So the lesson isn't anti-knowledge. Sikhs value learning; Japji itself is full of it.
It's about the edge of knowledge, and the honesty to stand there and say: I don't know, and the Maker does.

how: Pauri 21 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; Sikh commentary reads its lines on the pandits, qazis and yogis to say that the beginning of creation is known only to the Creator.

o: the hour when the world began

s: Pauri 21 mocks the scholars it names
it names pandits, qazis and yogis evenly and says the answer is beyond them all.
Pauri 21 asks the hour, day, season and month of creation
like filling out a birth certificate for the universe.
Pauri 21 says the Maker who shaped creation alone knows
jaa kartaa sirathee kau saaje aape jaanai soee.

games.q: you're asked the exact day and hour the world began. what does Pauri 21 say?
o: the Maker who shaped it alone knows.
games.why: no pandit, qazi or yogi found the moment. the Maker who shaped creation alone knows.

practice: Think of one thing you've been pretending to know, or worrying about because you don't: how something will turn out, why something happened, what someone else is thinking.
Quietly say to yourself, I don't know, and notice what happens in your body; some tightness might loosen. Breathe with that, and let not knowing be allowed.

wordCard.voice: Kartaa, the Maker. No pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour the world began; the Maker who shaped creation alone knows.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kartaa, the Maker, the Creator; in Pauri 21, the only one who knows when creation began.

carryVoice: Your line: only the maker knows. The pandit, the qazi and the yogi all stand at the same edge. That's the week.
